passage:
Santosh,

Your message came on Tuesday, and I've read it maybe twenty times. "Sid, I know it's been six years. I've missed you. Can we meet?"

I want to be honest, because I think that's the only way this works. My first feeling was happiness. I actually laughed out loud in the metro. My second was something harder. When my father was in hospital in 2020, I called you and you never called back. I waited a long time for that call.

I'm not writing this to punish you. I don't need an explanation today. But I can't pretend the six years didn't happen, and I don't think you'd want me to.

So yes, let's meet. Sunday, at the old Irani café near college? Let's have chai and see who we are now. Maybe it'll be easy. Maybe it'll take a few Sundays. I'm willing to find out.

Siddharth

qa.a: Six years had passed.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Siddharth have about Santosh's message?
qa.a: Siddharth felt happy first, then a harder hurt and some resentment about the unanswered call years ago.

qa.q: How does Siddharth balance warmth and honesty in the reply?
qa.a: Siddharth agrees to meet warmly, names the old hurt plainly without punishing, and lets trust rebuild over a few Sundays.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel reading this reply?
qa.a: Santosh may feel relieved to be welcomed and a little ashamed about the missed call, but grateful for the honesty.

passage:
You want to know about Damini? Okay. I'm Omkar, and this is the story of the girl who vanished and came back.

We were best friends through engineering. After graduation she moved to Hyderabad, got engaged, and just... faded. Four years. Not even a reply to my birthday wishes.

Then last month: "Omkar, I'm in Pune this weekend. Coffee? I owe you an explanation."

I was thrilled, honestly. I was also angry, which surprised me. Part of me wanted to reply "Oh, NOW you remember me?"

I didn't. I went. She told me her engagement had ended badly and she'd pulled away from everyone. I listened. Then I said, "I'm really glad you're here. And it hurt, when you disappeared." She said, "I know. I'm sorry."

We're texting again, carefully. I'm not pretending the gap wasn't there. I'm not making her pay for it either. We're just going slow.

qa.q: How long had Damini been out of touch?
qa.a: She had been out of touch for four years.

qa.q: What did Omkar feel when Damini's message arrived?
qa.a: Omkar felt thrilled and, surprisingly, angry too, tempted to reply sarcastically.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's choices at the coffee meeting helped, and why?
qa.a: Omkar listened to Damini's reasons, said he was glad she was back, and honestly named that her disappearing hurt, without punishing her.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt coming to meet Omkar?
qa.a: Damini was probably nervous and ashamed, knowing she owed him an explanation after four years.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone whose old friend returns after years, feeling pleased, wary and a little resentful, meeting her with warmth and honesty and letting trust return slowly.

The lunch table in the audit firm's canteen went quiet when Gurleen sat down. Then Ashwin said, too brightly, "Don't worry, lots of people fail the CA final three times."

Gurleen's fork stopped. She had told exactly one person that: Pooja, on the office terrace, crying, two weeks ago.

She felt her face burn. She wanted to throw her tray at the wall. Instead she left, went to the stairwell and shook for five minutes.

At four o'clock she asked Pooja to step into the small meeting room. Her voice was low and steady. "I told you about my exam in confidence. Now the whole team knows. I felt humiliated in front of everyone. I need you to understand how much that hurt."

Pooja went white. "I thought I was helping, that they'd be kind..." She stopped. "No. That's an excuse. I'm sorry. I'll tell them it was private and I shouldn't have said it."

Gurleen nodded slowly. She would watch what Pooja did next.

qa.a: He said lots of people fail it three times.

qa.a: Gurleen felt humiliated and enraged, her face burning, wanting to throw her tray.

passage:
Dilnaz,

I'm writing this because if I call, I'll shout, and I don't want to.

On Saturday, three people from our college group messaged me about my parents' divorce. You're the only one I told. I told you at 2 a.m. on your terrace, and I said, "Please, nobody else." You promised. You always introduce me as your rakhi brother.

I've felt sick since then. Humiliated. So angry my hands shook reading those messages. Kunal's "so sad bro" with a hug emoji made me want to throw my phone in the sea.

I'm not ending our friendship in this letter. I'm telling you plainly what happened and how much it hurt. What I need now is for you to tell me honestly how it spread, to tell those three it wasn't yours to share, and to not do it again.

What you do next will decide what we are. Not my anger today. Your repair.

Jeevan

By morning, lying on a mattress in his uncle's house, he felt sick. Dolma hadn't even told her parents. Her cousins had.

He checked the time. Dolma's bus from Gangtok got in at ten. Her parents would be at the wedding lunch by twelve.

He was at the bus stand at nine-forty, stomach in knots. When she stepped down, he said it before she could smile. "Dolma, last night I told your cousins about the design school. I'm so sorry. There's no excuse. I wanted you to hear it from me before lunch."

She stared. Then she said, "I need to go find my mother. Don't follow me." He didn't.

In the Toronto restaurant where they both worked, Alejandro had told the head chef, just in passing, that Mei was planning to leave for pastry school in the autumn. He hadn't meant harm. He'd been trying to explain why she was always tired.

Now, an hour later, the chef was calling Mei into the office, and Alejandro felt his stomach turn over. She hadn't decided yet. She hadn't told anyone but him.

He had maybe two minutes. He caught her by the walk-in fridge. "Mei, wait. I told Chef about pastry school. It was my fault. I'm really sorry. I didn't want you walking in there blind."

Mei's eyes went hard. "You what?"

"No excuse. I'm sorry."

She took a breath and went into the office. Afterward she walked past him without a word. For two weeks she swapped her shifts away from his. Alejandro let her. On the third week, she said good morning.

passage:
Sonali, you think chai-time talk is harmless. Let your Aparna aunty tell you what I learned at twenty-four.

I worked at the post office in Pune. Every afternoon we three clerks sat with chai, and the best currency at that table was other people's troubles. One day I told them that our colleague Hemlata's husband drank, and that she came to work with swollen eyes. She had told me that alone, by the photocopy machine.

The other two leaned in. I felt so included. So close to them.

That evening I saw Hemlata at the bus stop, and she smiled at me. Just smiled. And I felt ashamed right down to my shoes.

That was my turning point. I asked myself: would she want this told? Of course not. From then on, at chai, I talked about my own things: my mother, my silly poems. The table got a bit quieter. But the friendships I made were real ones.

qa.a: She told her by the photocopy machine.

qa.a: She felt included and close to them in that moment.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Aparna's story?

qa.q: How might Hemlata have felt if she had known what was said at chai?

The canteen at the software park was deafening at four, and Lalit had exactly ten minutes before his next call. Varsha and Nikhil from his team were already leaning over their cutting chai.

"Did you hear about Tejas?" Varsha whispered. "He's been so weird lately."

Lalit knew why. Tejas had told him last Friday, in the parking lot, that his wife had moved back to her parents'. The words were right there in Lalit's mouth. It would make him the one who knew. It would feel like bonding.

He stopped. Would Tejas want this told over chai to people he barely knew? Obviously not.

"No idea," Lalit said. "Maybe just a rough patch. Anyway, I've got to tell you, my landlord is threatening to paint my room pink."

They laughed. Nikhil asked how his house hunt was going, and Lalit told them, honestly, how badly it was going. The ten minutes flew. Tejas's secret stayed where it belonged.

At the women's hostel near the university, Zainab and Sangeeta shared a room with one working fan. At midnight Sangeeta sat up in bed. "Can I tell you something? You can't tell anyone."

She had quit her PhD programme four months ago. She was working at a bookshop. Her parents in Raipur still thought she was writing her thesis. "Every Sunday call, I lie. I don't know how to stop."

Zainab felt the weight of it settle on her chest. "I won't tell anyone. I promise."

Two days later, Sangeeta's mother called Zainab's phone: Sangeeta wasn't picking up. "Is she working hard, beta? Is the thesis going well?"

Zainab's heart pounded. She didn't lie, and she didn't tell. "Aunty, she's safe and she's fine. Please ask her yourself; she'll call you tonight."

Then she went to Sangeeta. "I kept it. But it's getting heavy for you. Want to practise telling them? I'll sit with you."

Shalini,

I'm writing this the morning after, because I don't want you to think I've forgotten or that I'll act strange.

Last night you showed me the bruises on your arm and told me Rohit has pushed you before. You made me promise not to tell anyone. I've kept that promise. I haven't told your family or our friends, and I won't without asking you.

But I'm glad of what we did before you slept. We called the women's helpline together from my balcony, and the counsellor told you calmly that this is not your fault, and that you don't have to decide everything tonight. You stayed at my place. That was the right call.

Today, the counsellor has a slot at four. I'll take the afternoon off and come with you. If you ever feel unsafe, come here, any hour, no questions.

This isn't me being dramatic. It's me being your friend.

Deepak

In the small town of Bhor, everybody knew everybody, which was why Ritu came to Deepak's cycle shop after closing and spoke in a whisper. She was engaged to Sandeep, the wedding set for December. For two months she had been meeting someone else, a man from her office in Pune.

"If Sandeep asks, tell him I was at your mother's with you on Saturday. Please. You're my oldest friend."

Deepak's hands went still on the chain he was oiling. He felt torn in two. He loved Ritu like a sister. He also liked Sandeep, who had helped him fix the shop roof.

"I won't lie for you," he said quietly. "And I won't go and tell the whole town either. But I think what you're doing is wrong, Ritu. Sandeep deserves the truth from you, before December."

Ritu's eyes filled. "I thought you'd be on my side."

"I am. That's why I'm saying it."

passage:
Wednesday night.

Vishal called again. Third time this year. "Bhai, just need to crash at yours for a week, the landlord's being difficult." Last time a week became a month, and he left my fridge empty and my scooter with a flat tyre.

Before that: "Bhai, lend me eight thousand till Friday." Friday was in March.

When did he last call just to ask how I am? I honestly can't remember. When Papa was ill, he sent a thumbs-up.

I felt the old guilt rise, the voice saying a good friend never says no. Then I felt tired. Used, really.

So I said it, short: "Not this time, Vishal. I can't have anyone stay." He waited for the reasons. I didn't give any. He said, "Okay, wow," and hung up.

I'm Jatin, and I'm allowed to have a small, quiet flat. I'll still wish him on his birthday. But a friend who only calls for favours isn't much of a friend.

passage:
Counselling note, week four. Elizabeth, 25.

Elizabeth came in holding her phone. Her friend Salma, who last year told Elizabeth's ex-boyfriend private things about her family, has now sent a long apology. Elizabeth read parts of it aloud. It was sincere. Elizabeth's hands were tight around the phone as she read.

"She says she's changed. I want to believe her. I also feel sick when I think of having coffee with her like before."

I asked whether forgiving Salma and being close to her again had to be the same thing. Elizabeth looked surprised. She said she could let go of the anger, and maybe had already begun to, but that trust would take time.

We discussed a middle path: replying kindly, accepting the apology, and seeing Salma in groups for a while rather than one-to-one. Elizabeth said this felt right, and her shoulders loosened for the first time in the session.

Next session: check how the reply went.

qa.q: What did Salma tell Elizabeth's ex-boyfriend?
qa.a: She told him private things about Elizabeth's family.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling as she read the apology aloud?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt torn, wanting to believe Salma but still sick at the thought of being close like before.

qa.q: What middle path did Elizabeth choose, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Accepting the apology kindly but seeing Salma in groups for a while, so trust can be rebuilt through actions over time.

Tuesday, 11 p.m.

Nirmala finally apologised today. In the office pantry, cornered by the kettle, eyes red. "Ira, I'm sorry. I told Mehta sir you were interviewing elsewhere because I was jealous. It was horrible."

I believed her. That's the strange part. She meant every word.

And I still didn't know what to say. It was three months ago that Mehta sir took me off the Singapore project because of her. Three months of eating lunch alone.

What I said: "Thank you for saying it. I forgive you." I meant that too. I don't want to carry the anger anymore; it's exhausting.

What I didn't say: "Let's be friends like before." Because I don't know yet. Words are easy at a kettle.

So here's my plan. Friendly at work. Lunch together sometimes, if she wants. No secrets for a while. If she's still the person she says she is in six months, maybe more.

For tonight, lighter. A bit.

qa.a: She told him Ira was interviewing elsewhere.

qa.a: Ira felt torn: believing the apology and forgiving her, but still unsure and cautious about trusting her again.

Avni, you keep saying your friend "just gets upset easily". Let your Devika mausi tell you about Bharti.

We were twenty-three, both teachers at the same school. Whenever I wanted to do something without her, a cousin's wedding, a weekend at my sister's, Bharti would go silent. Two days of silence, then a sigh: "It's fine. I'm used to being left." And I'd cancel. Every time. I felt guilty and confused and I couldn't even say why.

The turning point was my sister's baby shower. Bharti sulked. I nearly cancelled. Then I heard myself thinking, Why am I scared of my own friend?

So I said, calmly, "Bharti, when I make plans without you, you go quiet until I give in. I'm going to the shower. I'll see you Monday."

She didn't speak to me for a week. I let her. I didn't chase. Slowly, I made other friends. Some patterns you can't fix. You can only step out of them.

qa.q: Whose baby shower did Devika want to go to?
qa.a: She wanted to go to her sister's baby shower.

qa.q: How did young Devika feel each time Bharti went silent?
qa.a: She felt guilty and confused, and ended up cancelling her plans.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Devika's story?
qa.a: At the baby shower plans she noticed she was scared of her own friend, named the pattern calmly, went anyway, and stepped back when Bharti punished her.

qa.q: How might Bharti have felt when Devika named the pattern?
qa.a: Bharti probably felt exposed and resentful, which may be why she stopped speaking to her for a week.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman whose friend used sulking and guilt to get her way, who named the pattern calmly, held her boundary and pulled back when punished.

Manoj's sister's engagement was at six on Sunday, and at eleven that morning Nikita called. "You promised to help me move. The truck's coming at four."

"I said I'd help Saturday, Nikita. I told you Sunday was the engagement."

A long, heavy sigh. "Right. Your family always comes first. I'll just do it alone. Like always."

Manoj felt the familiar knot. It had happened before: when he went to his friend's wedding, when he started gym. Each time, she went cold until he gave in. He had never quite been able to say what was wrong.

Now, standing in his room with his kurta ironed on the bed, he saw it clearly.

"Nikita, every time I have a plan, you make me feel guilty until I cancel. I'm not cancelling. I helped on Saturday. I'll be at the engagement."

She hung up. That evening, as his sister exchanged rings, Nikita posted something bitter online. Manoj muted her and went back to dancing.

passage:
Let me tell you about the worst week of my working life. I'm Jahnavi, and three years ago Uday and I started a small organic snack company from my parents' garage. He was my college best friend. We did everything together, even fought about fonts together.

Last month I found out he had been meeting an investor alone. He'd told them he was the founder and I was "on the team". I found out from the investor's email.

My first reaction was panic. I wanted to shut down the company account, post on social media, walk away. I felt like a fool. Everything we'd built felt fake.

My mentor made me sit down. "The sting is real. The product is also real. Separate them."

So I did. I gathered every email, every invoice with my name. I asked Uday for a meeting with a lawyer present, to write down who owns what. I was sad, and I let myself be. I didn't make one big decision in panic.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi find out about Uday's investor meetings?
qa.a: She found out from the investor's email.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she found out?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt panic and betrayal, like a fool, as though everything they had built was fake.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi's mentor help her do?
qa.a: Separate the sting of betrayal from the real value of the work, so Jahnavi gathered facts, asked for a written agreement with a lawyer, and avoided panic decisions.

qa.q: How might Uday see his meetings with the investor?
qa.a: We can't be sure; he may have seen it as helping the company, but he chose to present himself as the only founder.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone whose co-founder and close friend broke their trust, who separates the sting from the work's value, gathers facts and documents agreements instead of panicking.

passage:
Monday. Farhan opened the company bank statement for the tea-delivery startup and saw it: three payments from the company account to Manoj's personal account, marked "consulting". No one had agreed to them. Manoj had been his friend since class eight. Farhan sat in the tiny office feeling the floor tilt. Was any of it real?

Wednesday. He almost called Manoj at midnight to shout. Instead he made a list: dates, amounts, the shareholders' agreement they had never properly finished. He spoke to their chartered accountant and asked what documents they needed.

The following Monday. Farhan met Manoj with the accountant present. "I need to understand these payments." Manoj went pale, then said he'd meant to explain. Farhan stayed calm. "Maybe. From now on, every payment needs both our signatures, and we sign the agreement this month."

That night Farhan felt sad, not panicked. The friendship was bruised. The business, and the customers who loved their tea, were still real.

qa.q: How were the payments to Manoj's personal account marked?
qa.a: They were marked "consulting".

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he first saw the payments?
qa.a: Farhan felt shocked and betrayed, as if the floor was tilting, doubting that any of it was real.

qa.q: What did Farhan do instead of calling Manoj at midnight?
qa.a: He gathered facts, spoke to the accountant, and later met Manoj with the accountant present to set two signatures and a written agreement.

qa.q: How did Manoj react when Farhan asked about the payments?
qa.a: Manoj went pale and said he had meant to explain, which suggests he was caught out and uneasy.

grounding: The story shows a young man whose co-founder and old friend misused company money, who separates the sting from the business's value, gathers facts and documents agreements calmly.
